But we shall speak more precisely of these when the discourse proceeds in order to the treatment of the aids of <term>induction</term> <gloss>the process of deriving general principles from particular facts</gloss>.</meta>

XLIII. Among the prerogatives of instances we shall place in the twentieth position the instances of piercing; which we are also accustomed to call <term>twinging instances</term> <gloss>instances that pluck or provoke the intellect</gloss>, but for a different reason. For we call them <term>twinging</term> because they twinge the intellect; and <term>piercing</term> because they pierce through nature, from which we also sometimes call them the instances of Democritus. These are the instances which admonish the intellect of the admirable and exquisite subtlety of nature, so that it may be excited and awakened to proper attention, observation, and inquiry. For example: that a small drop of ink can be extended to so many letters or lines; that silver, gilded only on the outside, can be extended to such a length of gilded wire; that a tiny worm, such as is found in the skin, possesses within itself a spirit and a shape dissimilar to its parts; that a little saffron can color a whole cask of water; that a little civet or spice can scent a much larger volume of air; that from a small

<summary>Bacon introduces the twentieth prerogative, the "instances of piercing," which serve to awaken the intellect to the subtle nature of reality through examples of extreme physical division and efficacy.</summary>
